questions.question: 1. Which of these best describes an array in C/C++?

answers.a: A data structure that shows a hierarchical behaviour
answers.b: A container of objects of similar types
answers.c: A container of objects of mixed types
answers.d: A structure in which elements must be accessed using links

explanations.a: Incorrect. Hierarchical organization is associated with structures such as trees rather than arrays.
explanations.b: Correct. An array stores a collection of elements of the same data type in contiguous memory locations.
explanations.c: Incorrect. A conventional C/C++ array is designed to store elements of one declared data type.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Accessing elements through links is characteristic of linked structures rather than arrays.

questions.question: 2. What is the worst-case time complexity of insertion at an arbitrary position in an array?

explanations.a: Correct. Inserting at an arbitrary position may require shifting a linear number of elements.
explanations.b: Incorrect. A single insertion does not require a quadratic number of element shifts.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Sorting-style logarithmic factors are not involved in a single arbitrary-position insertion.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The number of elements that may need to be shifted can grow with the array size.

questions.question: 3. Which of the following is an invalid one-dimensional array declaration in C?

explanations.a: Incorrect. This declaration specifies an integer array with 1000 elements.
explanations.b: Incorrect. This declaration specifies a character array with two elements.
explanations.c: Correct. An array declaration requires array brackets; the shown statement does not declare an array.
explanations.d: Incorrect. This is a valid declaration and initialization of an integer array.

questions.question: 4. In a singly linked list, each node contains a minimum of two fields. If one field is the data field to store the data, then the second field is _______.

answers.d: Pointer to the last node only

explanations.a: Incorrect. A singly linked list does not normally maintain a backward link in each node.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The head is a reference to the first node and is not normally stored as the second field of every node.
explanations.c: Correct. The link field stores a reference to the next node in the singly linked list.
explanations.d: Incorrect. A node's link field is used to maintain the sequence of nodes rather than to point specifically to the last node.

questions.question: 5. In a singly linked list without a tail pointer, what is the asymptotic time complexity to add a tail element and to find an element?

explanations.a: Correct. Without a tail pointer, reaching the end can require traversing the list, and searching may also require traversal.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Without a tail pointer, reaching the last node generally requires traversal.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Searching an unsorted singly linked list may require examining multiple nodes.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Neither operation is guaranteed to take constant time under the stated conditions.

questions.question: 6. Why do we need pointers in a linked list but not in an array?

answers.b: Nodes in a linked list are not required to occupy contiguous memory locations
answers.c: Every linked-list node must store two arrays
answers.d: Arrays cannot support dynamic memory allocation

explanations.a: Incorrect. Dynamic allocation can also be used for arrays, so it is not the distinguishing reason.
explanations.b: Correct. Linked-list nodes may be located at different memory addresses, so links are used to connect the nodes.
explanations.c: Incorrect. A linked-list node does not require arrays as part of its basic representation.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Arrays can also be dynamically allocated in C/C++.

questions.question: 7. Which data structure follows the Last In, First Out principle and is commonly used to implement a stack?

explanations.a: Incorrect. A queue follows a First In, First Out access discipline.
explanations.b: Incorrect. A graph represents relationships among vertices and edges rather than a LIFO access discipline.
explanations.c: Correct. A stack follows the Last In, First Out principle, so the most recently inserted element is accessed first.
explanations.d: Incorrect. A tree represents hierarchical relationships and does not inherently impose LIFO ordering.

questions.question: 8. Which pair of operations is associated with inserting into and removing from a queue?

explanations.a: Incorrect. These operation names are conventionally associated with stacks.
explanations.b: Correct. Enqueue adds an element to a queue, while dequeue removes an element according to FIFO order.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Search is used to locate an element and is not the standard removal operation for a queue.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Peek and traversal describe access or inspection activities rather than the standard insertion and deletion pair for queues.

questions.question: 9. A stack contains the elements 10, 20, and 30, where 30 is at the top. If one pop operation is performed followed by push(40), which element will be at the top?

explanations.a: Incorrect. This element is below the other remaining stack elements and is not affected by the stated top operations.
explanations.b: Incorrect. This element remains in the stack but is not the element most recently pushed.
explanations.c: Incorrect. This element is removed by the pop operation before the new element is inserted.
explanations.d: Correct. The pop removes the previous top element, and push(40) places 40 at the top.
